before: One of the most important things to understand about whiplash is that symptoms are frequently delayed. It is not uncommon for an accident victim to feel fine at the scene only to develop significant neck pain, headaches, or cognitive difficulties days or even weeks later. This is why medical professionals and attorneys alike recommend seeking a medical evaluation immediately after any accident — even if you feel no pain at the time.
after: One of the most important things to understand about whiplash is that symptoms are frequently delayed. It is not uncommon for an accident victim to feel fine at the scene only to develop significant neck pain, headaches, or cognitive difficulties hours or even a day or two later. In one study of neck sprains after car accidents, neck pain had begun in 65 percent of patients within 6 hours, 93 percent within 24 hours and all of them within 72 hours (Deans et al., Injury, 1987). This is why medical professionals and attorneys alike recommend seeking a medical evaluation immediately after any accident — even if you feel no pain at the time.

before:
Medical professionals classify whiplash injuries using a standardized grading system developed by the Quebec Task Force in 1993. The severity grade assigned to your injury directly affects how your claim is valued, because higher grades generally involve longer recovery periods and greater medical expenses.

Grade Symptoms Physical Signs Typical Recovery
Grade 0 No neck complaints or physical signs None visible Monitoring recommended
Grade 1 Neck pain, stiffness, or tenderness only No physical signs at initial exam Weeks to months
Grade 2 Neck pain plus musculoskeletal signs Decreased range of motion, point tenderness Months; may require physical therapy
Grade 3 Neck pain plus neurological signs Decreased reflexes, weakness, sensory deficits Months to years; may require extensive treatment

A Grade 1 whiplash injury that resolves within a few weeks will be valued significantly differently from a Grade 3 injury that causes chronic pain and limits your ability to work. When you pursue a claim, your medical records documenting the grade and progression of your injury become some of the most critical evidence your attorney will use to calculate the full value of your case.
after:
Medical professionals classify whiplash injuries using a standardized grading system published by the Quebec Task Force on Whiplash-Associated Disorders in 1995. The severity grade assigned to your injury directly affects how your claim is valued, because higher grades generally involve longer recovery periods and greater medical expenses.

Grade Symptoms Physical Signs
Grade 0 No neck complaints or physical signs None visible
Grade I Neck pain, stiffness, or tenderness only No physical signs at initial exam
Grade II Neck pain plus musculoskeletal signs Decreased range of motion, point tenderness
Grade III Neck pain plus neurological signs Decreased reflexes, weakness, sensory deficits
Grade IV Neck pain plus fracture or dislocation Fracture or dislocation

The Quebec classification does not assign recovery times to each grade. The Neck Pain Task Force's review of the evidence found that about half of people with Grade I to III whiplash still report neck pain a year after the injury, and that greater initial pain, more symptoms and greater initial disability predict a slower recovery (Carroll et al., Spine, 2008).

A Grade I whiplash injury that resolves within a few weeks will be valued significantly differently from a Grade III injury that causes chronic pain and limits your ability to work. When you pursue a claim, your medical records documenting the grade and progression of your injury become some of the most critical evidence your attorney will use to calculate the full value of your case.

before: This is the most common approach for calculating non-economic damages. Your total economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, etc.) are multiplied by a factor — typically between 1.5 and 5 — based on the severity and duration of your injury. A mild Grade 1 whiplash that resolves in weeks might warrant a multiplier of 1.5 to 2, while a Grade 3 injury with chronic symptoms and ongoing treatment could justify a multiplier of 4 or higher.
after: Under this approach, your total economic damages (medical bills, lost wages, etc.) are multiplied by a factor based on the severity and duration of your injury. Neither Georgia nor South Carolina law prescribes this or any formula for pain and suffering; it is an informal convention adjusters and attorneys use in negotiation, and a jury is never bound by it.

before:
Under this approach, a daily dollar amount is assigned for every day you experienced pain and limitations from your whiplash injury. For example, if a daily rate of $150 is applied over a 180-day recovery period, the non-economic damages would total $27,000. This method is sometimes used for injuries with a clear recovery timeline.

What Settlement Ranges Look Like

Whiplash settlement amounts vary widely depending on the facts of each case:

  • Mild whiplash (Grade 0–1) that resolves within weeks: $2,500 to $10,000
  • Moderate whiplash (Grade 2) requiring physical therapy and months of treatment: $10,000 to $50,000
  • Severe whiplash (Grade 3) with chronic pain, neurological symptoms, or long-term disability: $50,000 to $150,000+

These ranges are general estimates. The actual value of your claim depends on your specific medical evidence, the strength of the liability case against the at-fault party, and the insurance policy limits available. An experienced car accident attorney can evaluate your case and provide a realistic assessment of what your whiplash claim is worth.

State Filing Deadline Statute
Georgia 2 years from the date of injury O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33
South Carolina 3 years from the date of injury S.C. Code § 15-3-530

While these deadlines may seem like plenty of time, building a strong whiplash claim requires gathering medical records, documenting your treatment history, negotiating with insurance companies, and potentially retaining expert witnesses. Starting the process early gives your attorney the best opportunity to maximize your compensation. Claims against a government entity run on different clocks. In Georgia, a written ante litem notice is due within six months for a city (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5) and within 12 months for a county (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1) or the state (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26). South Carolina requires no pre-suit notice, but its Tort Claims Act shortens the filing deadline to two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110). Speak with an attorney as soon as possible to ensure your rights are protected.
